summary:
An essay from Charter, written by a facilitator of off-the-record chief people officer forums, argues that AI-era "machine pace" is burning out the highest performers companies fought hardest to retain. One CPO describes top performers as "trying to outrace irrelevance." The author says this moment differs from prior disruptions in three ways: there is no defined end state (employees at Zapier ask "transformation into what? When are we done?"), even habitual fast learners cannot keep up with learning new ways of working on top of existing jobs, and the pain is no longer shared because the disruption is internally driven by leaders who sit furthest from the fallout.

The piece traces how pressure travels: boards question why AI investment is not paying off faster, which becomes HR-enforced mandates to use AI on every project. A product designer recounts spending one hour building a Figma prototype and fifteen hours fighting an AI tool to reproduce it, and being told to build everything as AI prototypes to prove AI's worth to an investor; she left tech.

The author argues executives do not see the maintenance tail of AI output, the code that must be secured, documented and maintained, and cites SurveyMonkey data showing leaders query AI three times as often as reports and are three times as likely to accept answers without validation. Managers under deadline choose to fix AI errors themselves rather than coach juniors, so apprenticeship stops.

The conclusion frames burnout as a design choice, referencing BCG's "AI brain fry" and a Gensler finding on heavy AI users. Passing mentions include office attendance mandates, always-on messaging and 9-9-6 culture as symptoms of the same pace pressure. No workplace-technology, visitor management, or space booking content of substance.
